message.content: {"passages":[{"reference":"6.6","text":"The first-formed egg, then, warmed by the living creature within it, breaks open; next, once formed, the creature comes forth, just as Orpheus also says, “when the hard, capacious egg was split.” And so, when the one who had come forth appeared with great power, the shell receives its harmony and attains its ordered arrangement, while he himself sits enthroned as though on heaven’s highest ridge and, among mysteries, illumines the boundless age from all sides. But as for the fertile matter left behind inside the shell: as it lay there over a long time, natural heat simmering beneath it separated out the substances of all things. For its lowest part had first sunk downward under its weight, like sediment. Because of its downward-dragging quality and because of the weighty and great mass of the substance lying beneath, they named it Pluto, declaring him to be king of Hades and the dead.","lexical_decisions":[{"source_quote":"τὸ μὲν οὖν πρωτοσύστατον ὠὸν","chosen":"The first-formed egg, then","rationale":"πρωτοσύστατον describes what was constituted or formed first; “primordial” is possible but less transparent."},{"source_quote":"κραναίου σχισθέντος πολυχανδέος ὠοῦ","chosen":"when the hard, capacious egg was split","rationale":"κραναίου is taken as “hard” or “hard-shelled,” while πολυχανδέος denotes great capacity; “wide-gaping” is a possible alternative for the latter."},{"source_quote":"τὸ μὲν κύτος","chosen":"the shell","rationale":"κύτος denotes a hollow vessel or cavity; in the immediate egg imagery, “shell” best identifies the remaining enclosure."},{"source_quote":"ἐν ἀπορρήτοις τὸν ἄπειρον περιλάμπων αἰῶνα","chosen":"among mysteries, illumines the boundless age from all sides","rationale":"ἀπόρρητα can be secret or ineffable things, hence “mysteries”; περιλάμπων may mean either shining around something or illuminating it on every side."},{"source_quote":"διὰ τὴν ὁλκότητα","chosen":"because of its downward-dragging quality","rationale":"ὁλκότης conveys a tendency to pull or weigh downward; “heaviness” is possible but would duplicate the following ἐμβριθές."},{"source_quote":"ᾅδου τε καὶ νεκρῶν βασιλέα","chosen":"king of Hades and the dead","rationale":"The two coordinated genitives are both retained rather than treating “Hades” merely as an explanatory synonym for the dead."}],"source_issues":[{"source_quote":"ὡς ἐν πολλῷ τῷ χρόνῳ ὑποκειμένης ἕως φυσικῆς ὑποζέουσα ἡ θερμότης","issue":"The supplied reading is syntactically irregular: ὑποκειμένης lacks an unambiguous genitive head, while ἕως does not join smoothly with φυσικῆς and the nominative ἡ θερμότης. The translation gives the contextually recoverable temporal relation and treats the sentence as anacoluthic. A plausible conjecture is that ἕως arose for ὕλης, but that conjecture is not adopted as though it were the supplied text.","proposed_reading":"ὡς ἐν πολλῷ τῷ χρόνῳ ὑποκειμένης ὕλης φυσικῆς ὑποζέουσα ἡ θερμότης","blocks_publication":false}]},{"reference":"6.7","text":"This first and abundant, foul and rough substance, then, they say was swallowed by Cronus—that is, Time—in a natural sense, because of its downward descent. After the first sediment, they named the water that had flowed together and floated upon the first deposit Poseidon. The remaining third portion, the purest and uppermost, since it was transparent fire, they named Zeus because of the boiling nature within it. For since fire rises upward, it was not swallowed in the regions below by Time, Cronus; rather, as I said, the fiery substance, being life-giving and upward-moving, flew up into the air itself, which is also the most intelligent because of its purity. By his own heat, therefore, Zeus—that is, the boiling substance—draws up the most rarefied and divine breath left within the underlying moisture, which they called Metis.","lexical_decisions":[{"source_quote":"ὑπὸ Κρόνου τοῦ χρόνου","chosen":"by Cronus—that is, Time","rationale":"The rendering preserves the author’s identification and wordplay between Κρόνος and χρόνος rather than treating τοῦ χρόνου as an unrelated genitive."},{"source_quote":"φυσικῶς","chosen":"in a natural sense","rationale":"The adverb signals the physical or natural-philosophical interpretation of the myth; “by natural processes” is also possible."},{"source_quote":"διὰ τὴν κάτω ὑπονόστησιν αὐτῆς","chosen":"because of its downward descent","rationale":"ὑπονόστησις denotes a movement or return downward; “downward retreat” would preserve its etymological coloring but is less natural here."},{"source_quote":"τὴν πρώτην ὑποστάθμην","chosen":"the first sediment","rationale":"ὑποστάθμη denotes matter settled at the bottom; the related ὑποστάσει later in the sentence is rendered “deposit.”"},{"source_quote":"Ζῆνα ὠνόμασαν διὰ τὴν ἐν αὐτῷ ζέουσαν φύσιν","chosen":"they named Zeus because of the boiling nature within it","rationale":"The conventional name “Zeus” is used while the explicit sound association between Ζῆνα and ζέουσαν is retained through “boiling.”"},{"source_quote":"τὸ ἰσχνότατον καὶ θεῖον ἀνιμᾶται πνεῦμα","chosen":"draws up the most rarefied and divine breath","rationale":"In this physical account, ἀνιμᾶται describes drawing up or vaporizing, and ἰσχνότατον means exceedingly fine or tenuous rather than literally lean."}],"source_issues":[]},{"reference":"6.8","text":"When that breath reaches the crown of the ether himself and is compressed by him, like moisture mixed with heat, it produces an ever-moving pulsation and gives birth to understanding, which they also call Pallas because it pulses: a most skillful intelligence, by whose use the etherial craftsman fashioned the entire cosmos. From Zeus himself, who permeates everything—the hottest ether—the air reaches as far as the regions here; this they call Hera. And since it has descended beneath the purest substance of the ether and is feminine in purity by comparison with what is superior, it was reasonably regarded as Zeus’s sister, since it had been generated from the same substance, but as his wife because it lies beneath him as a woman does.","lexical_decisions":[{"source_quote":"κατὰ κορυφῆς δὲ αὐτοῦ ἐλθὸν τοῦ αἰθέρος","chosen":"When that breath reaches the crown of the ether himself","rationale":"The implicit subject is the divine πνεῦμα from 6.7. κορυφή can be the top, crown, or head; “crown” preserves both the cosmological height and the mythic head imagery."},{"source_quote":"τὸν ἀεικίνητον παλμὸν ἐνποιῆσαν","chosen":"it produces an ever-moving pulsation","rationale":"παλμός denotes a throbbing, quivering, or pulsation; this wording also supports the following etymological association with Pallas."},{"source_quote":"ἣν καὶ Παλλάδα ἐπονομάζουσιν διὰ τὸ πάλλεσθαι","chosen":"which they also call Pallas because it pulses","rationale":"The translation preserves the author’s wordplay between Παλλάδα and πάλλεσθαι without asserting that it is a historical etymology."},{"source_quote":"ὁ αἰθέριος τεχνίτης","chosen":"the etherial craftsman","rationale":"The adjective identifies the craftsman with or as belonging to the ether; “craftsman of the ether” is possible but may imply that the ether is merely his material."},{"source_quote":"τοῦ διήκοντος Διὸς","chosen":"Zeus himself, who permeates everything","rationale":"διήκω means to extend or pass through; “permeates everything” reflects the preceding description of Zeus as universally diffused."},{"source_quote":"ὡς θήλεια τὴν καθαρότητα, πρὸς σύγκρισιν τοῦ κρείττονος","chosen":"is feminine in purity by comparison with what is superior","rationale":"The accusative τὴν καθαρότητα marks respect: the air is characterized as female with respect to purity relative to the superior ether. “Less pure, and therefore female” would make the implication more explicit than the Greek does."},{"source_quote":"γαμετὴ δὲ διὰ τὸ ὡς γυναῖκα ὑποκεῖσθαι","chosen":"but as his wife because it lies beneath him as a woman does","rationale":"γαμετή means a wedded woman or wife, and ὑποκεῖσθαι retains both the physical placement of air beneath ether and the author’s gendered analogy."}],"source_issues":[{"source_quote":"ὁ ἀὴρ μέχρι τῶν ἐνταῦθα διικνεῖται τόπων, ἣν ἐπονομάζουσιν Ἥραν","issue":"The masculine antecedent ὁ ἀήρ is followed by the feminine relative ἣν. This can be understood as an anticipatory shift to the personified feminine name Hera rather than as missing content, so the translation uses “this” without emendation.","proposed_reading":"","blocks_publication":false}]},{"reference":"6.9","text":"Hera is taken to represent a temperate balance of airs, and for that reason she is also exceedingly fertile. Athena, whom they also call Pallas, was regarded as a virgin because, on account of the extreme heat, she could not produce the generation of anything. Artemis is interpreted similarly: they take her to represent the lowest recess of the air and, because she is barren through the extremity of the cold, they likewise called her a virgin. As something that clouds the mind, they name the turbid and intoxicating compound of vapors from above and below Dionysus. The water beneath the earth, though one in nature, passes through all the channels in the land and is divided into many parts—as though cut into pieces—so they called it Osiris. They also take Adonis to represent ripe fruits, Aphrodite mixture and generation, Demeter the earth, Kore seeds, and some take Dionysus to represent the vine.","lexical_decisions":[{"source_quote":"παραλαμβάνεται δὲ ἡ μὲν Ἥρα πρὸς ἀέρων εὐκρασίαν","chosen":"Hera is taken to represent a temperate balance of airs","rationale":"παραλαμβάνεται introduces an allegorical identification, while εὐκρασία is a well-balanced or temperate mixture rather than merely pleasant weather."},{"source_quote":"διὰ τὸ ἄκρως θερμὸν γένεσίν τινος ποιῆσαι μὴ δυναμένη","chosen":"because, on account of the extreme heat, she could not produce the generation of anything","rationale":"The rendering preserves both the extreme heat and the explicit inability to cause γένεσις; “bring anything into being” is a smoother alternative."},{"source_quote":"εἰς τὸν κατώτατον μυχὸν τοῦ ἀέρος","chosen":"to represent the lowest recess of the air","rationale":"μυχός is an innermost or remote recess; “lowest depth” is possible, but “recess” preserves the spatial image."},{"source_quote":"ὡς φρενῶν θολωτικὸν","chosen":"As something that clouds the mind","rationale":"φρένες can denote mind, understanding, or faculties, and θολωτικός means making turbid or confused."},{"source_quote":"τὴν ἀπὸ τῶν ἄνω τε καὶ κάτω ἀτμῶν θολερὰν καὶ μεθύουσαν σύστασιν","chosen":"the turbid and intoxicating compound of vapors from above and below","rationale":"σύστασις here is a combination or compound; μεθύουσαν may describe it as intoxicating or as itself drunken."},{"source_quote":"διὰ πάντων τῶν χερσαίων πόρων διείρον","chosen":"passes through all the channels in the land","rationale":"διείρον depicts passage or threading through, and χερσαίων specifies channels belonging to the land."},{"source_quote":"λαμβάνουσι δὲ καὶ Ἄδωνιν εἰς ὡραίους καρπούς","chosen":"They also take Adonis to represent ripe fruits","rationale":"ὡραῖος means produced in its proper season and hence ripe; “seasonal fruits” is an equally possible rendering."}],"source_issues":[]},{"reference":"6.10","text":"Understand all such things for me as likewise possessing some such allegory. Regard Apollo as the sun that makes its circuit, an offspring of Zeus, which they also called Mithras, completing the circuit of a year. Let these transformations be understood by you as the many changes of Zeus, who permeates everywhere, and conceive of his countless women as years or generations. For the power that passes through the air from the ether itself, consorting with every year and generation, changes it in different ways and thus produces or destroys the things of the season. The ripe fruits are called children, while the unions with males are the periods of barrenness that occur at certain seasons.","lexical_decisions":[{"source_quote":"νόει μοι","chosen":"Understand ... for me","rationale":"The ethical dative μοι adds a personal appeal such as “take it from me”; retaining “for me” preserves it without making the phrase overly colloquial."},{"source_quote":"Ἀπόλλωνα δὲ ἥλιον τὸν περιπολοῦντα εἶναι νόμιζε","chosen":"Regard Apollo as the sun that makes its circuit","rationale":"περιπολεῖν denotes going around or patrolling a circuit, fitting the sun’s recurring course."},{"source_quote":"γονὴν ὄντα τοῦ Διός","chosen":"an offspring of Zeus","rationale":"γονή can mean birth, offspring, or generative seed; the personal genealogy favors “offspring,” though “product of Zeus” is possible in the physical allegory."},{"source_quote":"ὃν καὶ Μίθραν ἐκάλεσαν","chosen":"which they also called Mithras","rationale":"The masculine relative most naturally refers to the sun identified with Apollo, though its proximity to Zeus makes the grammatical reference formally capable of momentary ambiguity."},{"source_quote":"αἱ πολλαὶ νοείσθωσάν σοι τροπαί","chosen":"be understood by you as the many changes","rationale":"τροπαί can be turnings, changes, or seasonal revolutions; “changes” distinguishes it from the preceding μεταμορφώσεις while retaining the sense."},{"source_quote":"τὰς δὲ μυρίας αὐτοῦ γυναῖκας ἐνιαυτοὺς ἢ γενεὰς ἐπινόει","chosen":"conceive of his countless women as years or generations","rationale":"μυρίας means countless or innumerable, and γενεάς may denote generations, ages, or successive periods."},{"source_quote":"ἑκάστῳ ἐνιαυτῷ καὶ γενεᾷ συνουσιάζουσα διαφόρως αὐτὸν τρέπει","chosen":"consorting with every year and generation, changes it in different ways","rationale":"συνουσιάζουσα preserves the sexual language underlying Zeus’s unions. The masculine αὐτόν most immediately permits reference to the air or to each year; “it” retains that referential ambiguity."},{"source_quote":"γεννᾷ ἢ φθείρει τὰ ὡραῖα","chosen":"produces or destroys the things of the season","rationale":"τὰ ὡραῖα denotes things belonging to or ripening in their proper season, including seasonal produce; “ripe things” would be narrower."}],"source_issues":[]}]}
